item.title: 04.kinematics
item.description:
We are not animals. We are not a product of what has happened to us in our past. We have the power of choice. Stephen Covey "اللهم إني أسألك فهم النبيين، وحفظ المرسلين، والملائكة المقربين، اللهم اجعل ألسنتنا عامرة بذكرك، وقلوبنا بخشيتك، إنك على كل شيء قدير" Kinematics = the geometry of motion, ignoring what causes it like power or torque It ignores forces, torques, and accelerations. Only position and velocity exist in this world. Anything about "will the battery handle this?", "how much torque does the motor need?", or energy belongs to dynamics, a different course topic. افترض إن عندك ذراع روبوت طوله مترين. في الـ Kinematics، تقدر تحسب مكان إيده لما تغيّر زوايا المفاصل، حتى لو مش عارف نوع الموتور المستخدم. لكن في الـ Dynamics، لما تطلب منه يشيل حمولة وزنها (5,kg)، محتاج تدرس العزوم والكتل والقصور الذاتي عشان تعرف هل الموتور يقدر ينفذ الحركة المطلوبة. It splits into two parts: Position kinematics: It relates joint angles and positions to the location and orientation of the robot's end effector. This is the core part we will be working on today.(This lecture) Differential (velocity) kinematics: This examines the relationship between joint velocities and the velocity of the robot's end-effector, often utilizing the Jacobian. This is an extension of the current lecture the detailed derivation is not covered here. (Next lecture) Why ignore forces? A robot arm is a chain of rigid links. Where its hand ends up depends only on the shape of the chain (link lengths and joint angles), not on how hard the motors pushed. So geometry alone answers "where is the hand?". Forward and inverse kinematics: ~={blue}Forward kinematics=~ (~={green}FK=~): "I know the joint angles. Where is the hand or end factor?" Maps ~={blue}Inverse kinematics=~ (~={green}IK=~): "I want the hand there. What joint angles do I need?" Maps: Why both matter in a real robot: the motors are commanded in joint space (~={brown}you send them angles=~), but you think and plan in task space ("~={brown}grab the cup at this position=~"). ~={green}IK converts your goal into motor commands=~. ~={yellow}FK converts motor readings back into "where is my hand now?",=~ which is needed for feedback. This is why the lecture opened with PID control the controller drives each joint, and kinematics tells it which joint values to aim for.
Take a planar arm with rotating joints. Knowing as and fully determines the arm's shape: is the Configuration Vector its contains joint position vector, with entries (one per joint). is angle measured from the ground/x-axis to link 1. is angle measured from the extension of Previous link, which is link 1 to link 2. It is a relative angle, not measured from the ground. Position Matrix: describes the end effector (the tool or hand) and has entries. In 3D, a rigid body has at most 6 DOF: 3 translations and 3 rotations . So . In 2D, at most 3: plus one rotation . So . The lecture gave useful examples of choosing based on the task: A car on a road: at most (position and heading). A train on a rail: (distance along the track). A ball you want to move: in 2D, because a ball has no "front", so orientation is irrelevant. You only track . You choose to contain only what the task cares about.
Configuration space = all possible values of in the space.
Task space = all possible values of in the space. Concrete picture from the lecture: if , the configuration space is a square, and one point in the square is one pose of the robot. (Strictly, since and are the same angle, it wraps around like a donut, a torus. A square is a fine first picture.)Forward Kinematics () calculates end-effector pose from known joint angles (), Inverse Kinematics solves the reverse mapping (). It is just evaluating a formula, which is why the lecturer called it easy.Inverse Kinematics () is a core problem in robotics that deals with finding the joint variables (angles for rotation joints, extensions for prismatic joints) required to place a robot's end effector at a desired position and orientation in task space. What is the end of the robot domain before even start just by math: Let’s think about this geometrically. We have two links with lengths and . An important point to note: in this lecture, the basic Inverse Kinematics problem deals only with and coordinates the orientation of the gripper is not necessarily specified. This is allowed because of the possibilities of multiple solutions for the same target position.
